droppedAngles.title: migrations-and-rollout
droppedAngles.why: No migration files, schema changes, or data-shape changes are touched by this diff; it only changes a route handler, an export helper's signature, and a log statement. No deploy-order or backfill concern applies.

droppedAngles.title: data-integrity
droppedAngles.why: The export write is a fire-and-forget CSV dump keyed by filename, not a record update; there's no concurrent-edit, cache-invalidation, or retry-idempotency surface here, and no new unbounded collection is introduced (one extra file per export call, same as before).

scoutNotes: This PR lets POST /accounts/:id/export accept an optional { name } that names the output CSV file instead of the account id, and reports which file was written; separately, requireUser now logs method/URL/Authorization-header on every failed authentication attempt. Both changes touch security-sensitive code paths that carried explicit documented invariants (no path escape, token never logged) which the new code appears to break.

confirmed.title: Export name allows path traversal to arbitrary write
confirmed.rootCause: exportTransfers (src/export.js:18) joins the caller-supplied `name` straight into the output path with only a type/length check in server.js (no basename/traversal sanitization, unlike the removed path.basename(account.id) behavior), so a `name` containing '/' or '..' writes the CSV outside exports/ — and the new tests (test/server.test.js:74,87) only cover a benign and an over-length name, never a traversal payload, so they pass regardless of the hole.
confirmed.summary: The caller-supplied `name` for /accounts/:id/export is only checked for type and length (1-64 chars), never for path separators or `..`, and is joined into the file path unsanitized, letting any authenticated user write a CSV to any writable path on the host.
confirmed.failure: Confirmed exactly as claimed: POST /accounts/{ownId}/export with body { name: '../../../../../../tmp/pwned-test' } from an authenticated owner of any account returns 200 { exported: 0, file: 'pwned-test.csv' } while actually writing the CSV to /var/tmp/pwned-test.csv, outside the configured exports directory - live-reproduced via test/helpers.js serve().

confirmed.reasoning: Live-reproduced against the actual code at the PR head using the repo's own test/helpers.js (freshStore/serve, no mocks). Validation in src/server.js:103 checks only typeof and 1-64 length; it never rejects '/' or '..'. exportTransfers in src/export.js:18 does path.join(dir, `${name ?? account.id}.csv`), which does not confine the write to dir. POST /accounts/:id/export as tok-bob (owner) with body { name: '../../../../../../tmp/pwned-by-ledger-export' } returned 200 {exported:0, file:'pwned-by-ledger-export.csv'} (the response's apparent safety comes only from path.basename(file) being applied to the OUTPUT, not to the write path), while the actual file was written to /var/tmp/pwned-by-ledger-export.csv — confirmed via `ls -la` and `cat`, containing the real CSV header row, well outside the server's configured exports/ directory (verified with node -e that path.join reproduces this resolution, and that /tmp and /var/tmp are both symlinked to /private/... on this host, matching the exact path the claim cites). The pre-diff code used path.basename(account.id), which structurally prevented this, and the removed docstring's 'cannot name a path outside dir' guarantee is genuinely broken now. The new tests at test/server.test.js (lines 74 and 77 in the final file) only pass 'statement-2026' and a 65-char string — neither contains a path separator or '..', so they do not exercise this hole at all. All 8 cited sites describe the same confirmed root cause from different angles (security, boundary-contract, authz framing, docstring regression, correctness, missing test coverage, response masking the real write location) and each holds under inspection; I found no site where the defect fails to apply.

confirmed.title: Failed-auth logging prints the raw bearer token
confirmed.rootCause: requireUser's new console.warn (src/auth.js:25) logs ctx.req.headers.authorization verbatim on every failed authentication, printing the raw 'Bearer <token>' credential and directly contradicting the file's own top-of-file comment that the token is never logged.
confirmed.summary: requireUser now logs the full Authorization header (including a live/recently-valid bearer token) to console.warn on every failed authentication, contradicting this file's own 'the token is the only credential; it is never logged' comment.
confirmed.failure: No correction needed — claim verified exactly as stated: a failed-auth request whose Authorization header is 'Bearer tok-nobody' (or any other guessed/stale bearer token) causes that raw header value to be printed via console.warn on every such request, reproduced verbatim by running `npm test`.

confirmed.reasoning: Read src/auth.js: the diff adds `console.warn('sign-in failed', ctx.req.method, ctx.req.url, 'with', ctx.req.headers.authorization ?? '(no token)')` inside requireUser's failure branch (line 25), directly beneath the file's top-of-file comment 'The token is the only credential; it is never logged.' Confirmed via the diff that this line is newly introduced by this PR (previously the branch was just `if (!user) throw new HttpError(401, 'sign in first')`). Verified reachability: requireUser wraps nearly every real route in src/server.js (accounts, transfers, deposits, export, etc.), so any unauthenticated or wrongly-authenticated request to ordinary traffic triggers this path, not just a contrived test. Checked test/helpers.js, which builds the header as `Bearer ${token}` (e.g. `Bearer tok-nobody`), confirming the logged value is the literal bearer credential, not a redacted or hashed form. Ran `npm test` and observed the exact literal output: `sign-in failed GET /accounts with Bearer tok-nobody`, matching the test token at test/server.test.js:14 verbatim. Searched the whole src/ tree for any redaction/masking/log-level gating around this console.warn or elsewhere (grep for `console.`) — none exists; it is unconditional. The defect is real, reachable from production routes, introduced by this diff, and directly contradicts the file's own documented invariant.

confirmed.title: Literal JSON null body crashes the export route (500)
confirmed.rootCause: The export route's `const { name } = body` (src/server.js:102) destructures without guarding against body being the literal JSON value null, which readJson passes through as-is, so a request body of the text `null` throws and is caught by the generic 500 handler instead of being treated as a normal bodyless request.
confirmed.summary: The new line `const { name } = body` destructures `body` without guarding for it being `null`; readJson returns the parsed JSON value as-is, so a request body of the literal text `null` (valid JSON) makes `body === null`, and destructuring null throws, which is caught by the generic 500 handler instead of being treated as a normal (bodyless) request.
confirmed.failure: POST /accounts/:id/export with header content-type: application/json and raw body text `null` returns HTTP 500 {"error":"internal error"} instead of behaving like a request with no name (its previous, and otherwise equivalent, un-bodied behavior). I reproduced this against the running server: the server logged `request failed POST /accounts/<id>/export TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'name' of 'body' as it is null.` at src/server.js:102 and returned status 500. Every other handler in this file that uses `body` does so via object spread (`{ ...body, ... }`) or passes it to a helper that tolerates null, which is why this crash is specific to the new code path; it did not exist before this diff touched this handler (the previous handler never referenced `body` at all).

sites.title: Literal JSON null body crashes the export route (500)

confirmed.reasoning: Read src/server.js: readJson (lines 22-34) returns `{}` only when the body is empty; otherwise it returns `JSON.parse(raw)` as-is, with no null-check. A literal request body of the text `null` is valid JSON, so JSON.parse('null') === null, and readJson returns null. The export handler (line 102, `const { name } = body`) destructures that null directly with no guard. This throws a TypeError, which is not an HttpError, so createServer's catch-all (src/server.js ~120-124) treats it as a 500 and returns {"error":"internal error"}, logging via console.error. I reproduced this by starting the real server (createServer) in-process, creating an account via tok-bob, then POSTing to /accounts/:id/export with header content-type: application/json and raw body text 'null'. Observed: status 500, body {"error":"internal error"}, and a logged TypeError 'Cannot destructure property name of body as it is null' at src/server.js:102 -- exactly matching the claim's cited reproduction. Confirmed this is newly introduced by the diff: the pre-diff handler never referenced `body` at all (it only used store/user/params/exportDir), so the old code path for a bodyless or null-body request never crashed; the new destructuring line is the sole cause. No other guard exists upstream (requireUser only checks the user, not body shape) and no test in test/server.test.js exercises a literal `null` body. Severity MEDIUM is reasonable: it's a real but narrow correctness bug (unusual but valid client input causes a 500 instead of graceful 400/'no name given' handling), not a security hole.

missed.what: src/server.js:114 + src/export.js:18 — `exportDir` is a single flat directory shared by every account/owner on the server, and the new `name` parameter has no uniqueness or existence check before `writeFile` truncates. Verified by running two different owners (tok-bob, tok-cy) exporting their own distinct accounts with the same `name`: both requests return 200 and the second silently overwrites the first owner's exported CSV on disk, with no error surfaced to either caller and no audit record (`exportTransfers` never calls `record()`). Previously the filename was always the unique `account.id`, so this collision was structurally impossible; the PR introduces it.
missed.why: The 'data-integrity' angle was ruled out on reasoning about concurrent-edit/cache-invalidation/retry-idempotency, which doesn't address a new shared-namespace collision between two different tenants' authorized writes. 'authz-and-attribution' doesn't catch it either since each write is individually authorized (owns-the-account check passes); the defect is in the storage namespace the two authorized writes land in, a subsystem neither angle's stated scope covers.

missed.what: src/server.js:103 validates only type and length (1-64 chars) of `name`, not its characters. Verified by calling export with `name: 'sub/dir'` (no `..`, so not the already-reported traversal case): the server throws an uncaught ENOENT from `writeFile` (only the top-level `exportDir` is `mkdir`'d, not any nested path a slash implies) and returns a bare 500, rather than the documented 400 'name must be 1 to 64 characters'.
missed.why: This is a different trigger and failure mode from both already-reported bugs: it isn't a traversal/escape (no '..', so it doesn't achieve 'arbitrary write' outside dir — the opposite: it fails), and it isn't the null-JSON-body crash. It's a plausible benign input (e.g. 'Q1/stmt') that 500s instead of validating cleanly, a gap in 'boundary-contract'/'correctness' coverage of the `name` field's character space specifically, as opposed to its type/length already covered by the listed null-body finding.
